gen-dafont-electroharmonix-gf-noto-sans-: Electroharmonix breaks every word into separate, commanding letters. Noto Sans Bengali follows with capitals barely taller than its lowercase and distinctly open mouths, so a long passage moves along smoothly beneath the display type.

Striking, gappy, and loud about it. Electroharmonix sets the tone with open-handed curves, while Noto Sans Buginese keeps its letter mouths open like unjoined chalk arcs and lets the heading do the shouting.

Commanding from the first glance, Electroharmonix is built for announcing, with gaps that split words into single letters. Noto Sans Buhid is built for reading, leaving generous room between curve ends and stems.

Noto Sans Cuneiform has an e that opens up instead of closing its eye, and a lowercase swollen like inflated glass beads. Electroharmonix, with its gapped and striking letters, makes the rounder body feel friendlier by comparison.

Noto Sans Gujarati ends its curved strokes before they turn inward, leaving large open counters in tall a, e and s. And Electroharmonix, with its split-up letters and open curves, takes the louder part while that body keeps things quiet.
